extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and researchers writing mathematical exposition (papers, notes, textbooks)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative criteria for clear mathematical writing and exposition (papers, lecture notes, textbooks, blog/wiki mathematical articles). Focuses on clarity, notation, organization, examples, and medium considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make it impossible to misunderstand
rubrics_metrics.description: We should not write so that it is possible for our readers to understand us, but so that it is impossible for them to misunderstand us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for maximal clarity: do not rely on readers to 'fill in' obscurities. Structure arguments so they force comprehension even if the reader's attention is distracted; choose phrasing and order that leave little room for misinterpretation (Quintilian / Butler translations cited as motivating maxim).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume non-linear reading; provide signposts
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume readers will read linearly or from beginning to end; include plenty of 'signposts'—pointers to where the reader has been and where they are going.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use forward/back references, summaries, and explicit roadmap sentences so a reader who jumps in mid-document or skims can still follow the structure and purpose of each part. Signposts help both wandering and linear readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use descriptive terms before using symbolic names
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a descriptive term before using the symbolic name for an object (e.g., 'the function f, the element x, the group G').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce objects first in words, then show the symbol; this orients readers and prevents confusion when symbols appear at sentence boundaries. Avoid beginning a sentence with a bare symbol where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remind readers of notation when reused after a gap
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't expect that your reader has internalized notation used earlier; when notation recurs after pages or sections, remind them of its meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you introduced Θ_{i,j,k}(x,y,z) on page 2 and reuse it on page 5, restate what subscripts and arguments indicate. Short reminders reduce cognitive load and prevent misreading of reused symbols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance abstraction and exemplification
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be a balance between abstract definitions and concrete examples; sometimes introduce a familiar example before a definition, other times give the abstract first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide case-by-case: for very familiar concepts (e.g., vector space) you might give abstract first then examples; for new concepts give an example first to convince the reader they understand. The goal is to make ideas feel natural and convincing, not to show off abstract generality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain the significance and explain results (write results down, not up)
rubrics_metrics.description: The goal of mathematical writing is to tell the world about a clever idea and explain why it is clever; 'Don't write your results up. Write your results down.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to make the reader feel they could have thought of the idea; present reasoning and motivation, not just terse formal statements. Emphasize intuition, motivation, and why the results matter in addition to formal proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vary sentence cadence and read aloud
rubrics_metrics.description: Vary cadence: intersperse long sentences with shorter declarative ones; read papers out loud to catch repetitiveness and awkward phrasing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long, idea-dense sentences should be broken up with short sentences to aid comprehension. Reading aloud helps identify repetitions, clumsy constructions, and places where flow is poor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose precise, context-appropriate words
rubrics_metrics.description: Search for the best and most precise word that maps to the context; be willing to favor precision and clarity (Halmos: prefer the best word).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer exact terms that convey the intended meaning; tasteful connotation can aid understanding, but avoid gratuitous or confusing poetic usages. The right word sets the correct frame for the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary synonym-swapping for mathematical objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid trying to find synonyms for the same mathematical object (calling a group a 'group' in one place and 'an action' later) if it causes confusion; context matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep consistent terminology for objects unless a deliberate, clearly-explained change of viewpoint is intended. Inconsistent naming can obscure meaning and confuse readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not start sentences with symbols; prefer words
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid beginning a sentence or phrase with a symbolic name where possible; it is bad form and harms readability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rephrase sentences to begin with words rather than symbols (e.g., 'The group G acts on X' rather than starting with 'G acts on X'). This preserves grammatical flow and keeps symbol-heavy passages readable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use examples strategically to convince and motivate
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes present a familiar example before a definition (to show comprehension), other times give the definition first; use examples to convince the reader they understand the concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples should illuminate why definitions are useful and how they apply; choose examples that are representative and familiar to your intended audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of medium: wikis/blogs vs journals (stability and peer review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wiki/blog-style writing has strengths (hyperlinking, rapid dissemination) but often lacks features of traditional journals: stable, citable versions and established peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If publishing on a mutable medium, consider how to provide stable citations (referencing revisions) and how to subject work to reliable review. Recognize that the choice of medium influences expectations about permanence and authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide clear structure and roadmaps for longer works
rubrics_metrics.description: For books, papers, or long notes, structure the work so readers can locate theorems/definitions reliably and the document can be referred to later without ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use numbered theorems/definitions, clear sectioning, and explicit references. If using mutable online media, indicate revision identifiers when citing specific results so references remain stable.
